slides.text: In 1956, a sculpture danced with a ballet company on Le Corbusier’s roof.
The sculptor Nicolas Schöffer built it with engineers from Philips and named it CYSP 1, for cybernetic and spatiodynamic.
Sixteen painted plates stood on a base with four rollers, and each plate turned on its own small motor.
Photoelectric cells and a microphone read the light, color and sound around it, and the plates and rollers moved in response.
That summer, the choreographer Maurice Béjart set his dancers beside it on the rooftop terrace of the Cité Radieuse in Marseille, to music by the composer Pierre Henry.
Magazines at the time called it the first cybernetic sculpture in the world.
